NurED article: *mālā (revision 3661)

Middle Indo-Aryan Source

*mālā n. f. 'wreath, garland, crown; row, line, streak'

Etymology of Source

  • Old Indo-Aryan mā́lā- n. f. 'wreath, garland, crown; row, line, streak'

Attested Gāndhārī Forms

+ *-kā-

  • ⟨malaa⟩ n. f. 'garland'
    [DoG]

⟨puṣpa⟩ 'flower' + m° + *-ikā-

  • ⟨puṣpamalia⟩ n. f. 'garland'
    [DoG]

+ *-ya-

  • ⟨malu⟩ n. m. 'garland'
    [DoG]

+ guṇa- 'type'

  • ⟨malaguṇa⟩ n. m. 'type of garland'
    [DoG]

Nuristani

  • Katë w kt mul, w kl/ne/se mol n. m. 'crown; comb, crest [of birds]; (monal pheasant) plume on headgear [pre-Islamic mark of honor for having killed enemies]; tassle' [also commonly used as an element in pre-Islamic personal names]
    [G X-3; S-kt; SA22; Grjunberg 1995b: 612; S-km]
Compound with māč 'man' + NKal. ẓ -odë, n -oda 'having' [lit. "having the plume of one man"]
  • Nur. Kalasha ẓ mačëmālodë́, n mačmālodá n. m. 'pre-Islamic killing rank for having killed one enemy, the mark of which was two monal pheasant feathers fixed to the headgear'[1]
    [T; Deg (⟨mačmalodˈa⟩); S-n (⟨mač-mâl-oda⟩)]
Compound [in the sense 'line'] with kṭë 'heel'
  • Katë se kṭë́-mol n. m. 'layer of goatskin around the bottom of traditional leather shoes'
    [S-km]
Compound [in the sense 'line'] with gul 'valley'
  • Katë se gal-mól n. m. 'river bank'
    [S-km]

+ *-ikā-

+ Tr. -k:
  • Tregami g mālík n. '(large) flower'[2]
    [ART]
Compound with kor 'ear'[3]
  • Katë se karmë́li n. f. 'earring'
    [S-km]
+ A. -k
  • Ashkun s karmalík n. 'earring'
    [B-w, S-s]

+ IA -in-/-in-ī 'having (m./f.)' (OIA mālín- 'garlanded, crowned') [apparently based on the comparison of the white forehead to a crest or crown]

  • Katë se mali n. 'element of livestock names used for animals with a white face'
    [S-km]
  • Prasun p māl/-i n. 'element of livestock names used for animals with a white face' [⇐ Kt.]; mālë́g n. 'female goat with a white face'
    [BD]
+ *-a-ka-/-ikā-[4]
  • Katë ne malén̆/malr̆ẽ́y (or malín̆/malr̆ĩ́y?), se malín̆/-i adj. '(of livestock:) having a white head/face and the rest of the body in a different color'
    [Grjunberg 1995b: 612 (⟨мала́нр̌⟩/⟨малр̌ḯǐ⟩); S-km]
  • Nur. Kalasha ẓ māln̩̆́; n mālẽ́ n. 'goat with a white forehead or head and a black body'
    [T; Deg]

Commentary

The presence of l in all languages shows that this is a loanword.

Footnotes

  1. ↑ Since the base word *māl 'crown, crest, plume' has disappeared in NKal., Tāza (2017) associates the term with māl 'possession, wealth' ⇐ Prs./Arab..
  2. ↑ This meaning seems to derive from the conception of mālā- as a flower garland, which is not apparent in Kt. mol, but widely attested in NIA. According to Abdul Rahman Tregami, mālik refers to larger flowers like roses (gulāb-mālik), which are rare in the Tregam area.
  3. ↑ Perhaps as "ear-flower" rather than "ear-garland".
  4. ↑ It is possible that some of the forms have been phonologically adapted to the set of livestock coat color terms with the suffix PNur. *-ena- + *-ka-/ikā-.

NurED article: *muṭṭa (revision 3727)

Middle Indo-Aryan Source

*muṭṭa adj./n. 'stunted, blunt, stumpy; stump'

Etymology of Source

  • Old Indo-Aryan mūrtá- adj. 'coagulated, solidified, settled into a fixed shape; stupefied, unconscious'

The meaning of the word may over time have been influenced by phonologically similar words like muṇḍa 'shaved, hornless, stunted, blunt', mūḍha- 'stupefied' and mūra/mūrkha 'dull, stupid', eventually resulting in its convergence with these into a loosely coherent group of variants in NIA (cf. CDIAL: T. 10187).

New Indo-Aryan Cognates

  • Pashai l muṭā́ adj. 'short'
    [IIFL III.3]
  • IA Kalasha muṭ n. 'plant, tree'
    [TC]
  • Gawar-Bati muṭha n. 'tree' [aspiration unexplained]
    [FLI-GB]

Nuristani

Compound with *kārr[ã]- 'ear'

  • Nur. Kalasha ẓ/n karmǘṭ n. 'ear, auricle'
    [T]

+ *-ka-/*-ikā- (adj.)

  • Katë w mëṭë́/-í, ne muṭë́/-í adj. 'short', se muṛë́/-í adj. 'short'
    [S-kt; SA22, S-km]
  • Prasun p/k müčóg adj. 'short' [⇐ Kt. + Pr. -og]
    [BD]

+ *-ka- (n.)

  • Katë w mëṭë́, ne muṭë́ n. m. 'large log; ancestor effigy (or idol) carved from a log'[1]
    [S-kt; G XIV-9; G I-1–2; SA22]
    • + -uk: w mëṭúk n. m. 'small log', ne muṭúk, se muṛúk n. m. 'log'
      [S-kt; KLD; S-km]
  • Nur. Kalasha ẓ müṭë́, n muṭá n. 'bush'
    [T; Deg]
  • Ashkun s moṭë́ n. 'newly sprouted nonwoody plant'
    [S-s]
    • + -uk: s muṭúk n. 'tree stump'
      [B-w]
  • Prasun p müčǘ n. 'large tree stump, block of wood; wooden idol' [⇐ Kt.]
    [BD, M-Pr]

Compound with *kārr[ã]- 'ear'[2]

  • Katë w karmë́ṭ(ë), ne karméṭë, se karmë́ṛi n. m. 'ear, auricle'[3]
    [G VIII-26; S-kt; KLD; S-km]
  • Ashkun s karmuṭë́ n. 'ear, auricle'
    [B-w, S-s (〈kârmoṭʹa〉)]

+ *-ra- (?)

  • Katë se muṛǘr adj. 'without branches, worn down'
    [S-km]

Compound with *kārr[ã]- 'ear' + *-ka-

  • Nur. Kalasha n kār-muṭurá n. 'ear, auricle'
    [Deg; S-n]

+ Kt. -vo (?)

  • Katë w mëṭó adj. 'dull, blunt'
    [S-kt]

Commentary

Widespread parallels in New Indo-Aryan make it likely that this is a loanword.

Footnotes

  1. ↑ It is not clear whether this word could also refer to idols in pre-Islamic times, or whether it was only used for ancestor effigies. In sources from Islamic times, it is used in both senses, but this may be due to retrospective misinterpretation from an Islamic perspective. Sun-Aro (2022) translates the word as Prs. but 'idol', and the narrator of Grjunberg's (1980) text I reports worship of carved mëṭë́ by a mythical ancestor. The same narrator also describes ancestor effigies with the term mëṭë́ and Klimburg (2008:397) confirms that muṭë́ was the general term for ancestor effigies among the eastern Katë. According to Palwal (1969: 140) "The Mate of Katavari [...] signifies effigy as well as idol". The etymological derivation from OIA mūrti- with 'idol' as its primary sense (proposed with reservations by Turner CDIAL: T. 10245) is, in any case, very doubtful. Most likely the sense 'log' is primary and Kt. mëṭë́ strō- as attested in G I-1–2 originally meant 'to carve a log (into an effigy)', before it became reinterpreted to also mean 'to carve an effigy'.
  2. ↑ Not, with CDIAL (T. 2837), from *karṇa-pattraka-. An analogous formation (with a first member < OIA karṇa-) is found in GB khamṭa 'ear'
  3. ↑ The final i of the se form is unclear, apparently not a feminine form. Perhaps it has been influenced by karmë́li 'earring'.

NurED article: *muṁdha (revision 2877)

Middle Indo-Aryan Source

*muṁdha n. m. 'forehead, head, top, chief, summit'

Etymology of Source

  • Old Indo-Aryan mūrdhán- n. m. 'forehead, head, top, chief, summit'

The MIA form may be based on the weak stem mūrdhn- > MIA *muṁnh° > *muṁdh° (cf. von Hinüber 2001: 202–203). If it derives from a variety without retroflexion of rt, rd(h), it could also be based on the nominative form. In that case, the development would be, roughly, OIA mūrdhā (nom.) > MIA muddha > muṁddha with "nasal condensation" (cf. Halfmann 2023b: 330) and a geminate plosive in the source form.

Middle Indo-Aryan cognates

  • Prakrit muddha, muddhāṇa, muḍḍha, muṁḍha, muṁḍhāṇa n. m. 'forehead, head, top, chief, summit'
    [PSM]

New Indo-Aryan cognates

  • IA Kalasha mun, mund n. 'the highest point of a mountain or hill or sky'
    [TC]

+ -ka-

  • Pashai kṛ mundā́ n. 'top of the head'
    [IIFL III.3]

Nuristani

  • Katë w/ne min; se mün n. m. 'forehead'
    [S-kt; SA22; S-km]
    • w míno e-; se mǘnë ye- v. 'to doze off, to sleep' [synchronically interpretable as 'to go with the forehead', with instr. forms of min ~ mün, but cf. also MIA *muṁdrā]
      [G XIV-16; S-km]
    • ne *Mésir-min; se *Mézir-mün n. 'name of the Tirich Mir'
      [Morgenstierne (1931: 444): ⟨Maisur Mun⟩, ⟨Meziri Min⟩]
  • Ashkun t mun n. 'rock' [< *'mountain peak' ?]
    [M-A ⟨muṇ⟩; M-A2 ⟨mun⟩]
  • Prasun ◊ münd n. 'summit, peak, high plateau; clan chief, (pre-Islamic) clan priest'
    [BD]

Commentary

A certain loanword, given the reflex of the IA development r̥H > ūr (cf. the inherited doublet *mārrānik(a)-).

It is not likely that Tr. modá 'neck' belongs here (as proposed by CDIAL: T. 10247), as this would entail an etymological separation from very similar words for 'neck' in the neighboring languages, on which see s.v. MIA *maṁdaga.

NurED article: *vāṇijjā̆ (revision 3465)

Middle Indo-Aryan Source

*vāṇijjā̆ n. n./f. 'trade'

Etymology of Source

  • Old Indo-Aryan vāṇijyā̆- n. n./f. 'trade, commerce'

Middle Indo-Aryan Cognates

  • Pali vāṇijjā- f. 'trade, trading'
    [PTSD]
  • Prakrit vāṇijjā̆- n./f. 'trade'
    [PSM]

Nuristani

  • Katë w v(r̆)ayíč, ne/se vr̆ẽč n. 'trade'
    • w vr̆ayíč ku-/bu-, ne/se vr̆ẽč ku-/bu- v. tr./itr. 'to sell/be sold'
      [G IX-26 (⟨vayī́č⟩); Mohammad (1991) (⟨wr̆aič⟩); KLD; S-km (adj. "for sale")]
  • Nur. Kalasha ẓ wn̩̆č bu- v. itr. 'to be sold'
    • Denominal verb: ẓ wn̩̆čëw-, n wr̆ẽčā- v. tr. 'to sell'
      [T; Deg]
  • Ashkun
    • Denominal verb: s/t waṇiċā̆- v. tr. 'to sell'
      [B-w; M-A]

Commentary

The phonological development gives no clear hints as to the inheritance status of these forms, but since the word family of OIA vaṇíj- 'merchant' is very common in later IA, but absent from Iranian, it is overall quite likely that they are IA loanwords in Nuristani (thus also CDIAL: T. 11230, 11233).[1]

Morgenstierne's (1973e: 234) hypothesis that Kt. vr̆ẽč results from contamination of OIA vikrīṇāti 'sells' with the etymon of H/U becnā 'to sell', is not necessary. Since the Kt. w form requires long *ā in the first syllable, MIA vāṇijjā̆- < OIA vāṇijyā̆- is the more likely source than the related synonym MIA vaṇijjā- < OIA vaṇijyā́- with a short root vowel.

The denominal verb stems appear to have been secondarily formed after final devoicing.

See also MIA vāṇiya from the same root.

Footnotes

  1. ↑ It may also be noted that at least in recent centuries the practice of trade has been considered uncharacteristic of Nuristani culture (see Cacopardo & Cacopardo 2001: 213, fn. 367; Azar 2006: 8, fn. 25).

NurED article: Vāṇiya (revision 3427)

Middle Indo-Aryan Source

vāṇiya n. m. 'merchant'

Etymology of Source

  • Old Indo-Aryan vāṇijá- n. m. 'merchant, trader'

Vr̥ddhi derivative of vaṇíj- n. m. 'id.'

Attested Gāndhārī Forms

  • ⟨vaniye⟩ n. m. 'merchants (dir.pl.)'

New Indo-Aryan Cognates

  • Gawar-Bati -wāni n. suff. 'collective suffix used with some kinship terms'
    [M-GB]
  • Pashai l -wānī n. suff. 'nominal suffix appearing in kō-ānī "from where", (u)wānī "from there", har-wānī "whosoever"'
    [IIFL III.3]

Nuristani

  • Katë w -vr̆ayi, ne/se -van̆i n. m. 'nominal suffix that derives nouns referring to people associated with a place, activity or property, demonyms, job titles and ownership titles' [f. form -vay, variant forms in cases of stress shift (cf. Halfmann 2024a: 110–115): w -vr̆éyi, ne -vr̆ẽ́y, se -vë́n̆i]
    [G IX-10; SA22; S-km]
  • Nur. Kalasha ẓ -wn̩̆, n -wr̆ẽ n. m. 'nominal suffix that derives nouns referring to people responsible for sth., or with authority over sth.; nominal suffix for collective forms of kinship terms; nominal (suffix) used as identifying pro-form akin to English 'one' in 'the one who is coming' or for superlatives ('the most X one')'
    [T; Deg]
  • Prasun wuni ~ wëni n. m. 'having' [proprietive nominal/adjectival element; synchronically not always analyzable as a suffix (Buddruss & Degener 2017: 108–109), cf. functionally Kt. -vo (Halfmann 2024a: 281–284)] [⇐ Kt.]
    [BD (⟨wuni⟩ ~ ⟨wənˈī⟩)]

Commentary

The characteristic northwestern MIA development -j- > -y- identifies this group of forms as loanwords.

Functionally, the development is similar to that of -pāla-(ka-) 'guardian' as a final member of compounds, which became a versatile nominal suffix over the course of IA history, referring to people associated with the base of derivation (Négyesi 2005) and was also borrowed into Nuristani (see pālaga). A comparable semantic development (though with much more limited productivity) happened with the English word/suffix (-)monger, which was extended from contexts like fish-monger to formations like war-monger.[1]

Judging from the overlapping semantic spectrum of the comparable suffixes in GB and Pash.,[2] it is possible that the functional reanalysis was already completed in the IA source language when the element entered Nuristani.

The origin of the Kt. feminine form is not fully clear. Perhaps it is identical with the feminine form of vo/vay 'having', secondarily associated with a form that was originally only masculine.

The derivation of Pr. wuni from PIIr. *-u̯ant- 'having' proposed by Buddruss & Degener (2015: 844) is phonologically problematic. It seems more likely that the suffix is borrowed from Kt., as proposed here, with specialization of its function to that of marking ownership and some functional convergence with the proprietives of the other Nuristani languages (Kt. vo/vay, NKal. oda/odi).

See also MIA *vāṇijja from the same root.

Footnotes

  1. ↑ While such a development is plausible in general, it is not necessarily the case that all functions of all the attested suffixes are etymologically derived from MIA vāniya. Some of them could be due to secondary homonymy with other etyma.
  2. ↑ The functional spectrum of the Pash. suffix is not well-documented enough for definite conclusions about its etymology.

NurED article: *śpāvi (revision 2744)

Middle Indo-Aryan Source

*śpāvi n. m. 'porcupine'

Etymology of Source

  • Old Indo-Aryan śvāvídh- n. m. 'porcupine' [lit. "dog piercer"]

Middle Indo-Aryan Cognates

  • Pali *sāvi n. 'porcupine' [mss.: ⟨sāmi⟩, ⟨sāsi⟩]
    [PTSD]
  • Prakrit sāviha n. 'porcupine' [< śvāvidha-]
    [PSM]

Nuristani

  • Katë w spay, se sabā́ (sabáy-) n. m. 'porcupine' [forms probably deformed by folk-etymological association with w spa-, se sabṓ- 'to sharpen (to a point; of arrows etc.)'), therefore s- instead of expected š]
    [S-kt; KLD; S-km]
  • Nur. Kalasha wg špey, ẓ šipéy, n/kg šapáy n. 'porcupine'
    [M-Wg (wg ⟨špēi⟩); T ('hedgehog'); Deg; S-n]
  • Tregami g špe n. 'porcupine'
    [ART]
  • Ashkun t šipā́ū n. 'porcupine'
    [M-A (⟨šipaˈũ⟩); M-A2]

compound of borrowed Kt. spay + borrowed reflex of OIA káṇṭa(ka)- 'thorn'?

  • Prasun p/d ispyḗkaṇṭ, z ispī́kaṇṭ n. 'hedgehog'
    [BD]

Commentary

A certain loanword with an IA palatal development (*ć > ś) and a Northwestern MIA phonological innovation (śv > śp).

Pace Morgenstierne (1942: 163) and Turner (CDIAL: T. 12766), Dam. ċuwā́r 'porcupine' is most likely unrelated to these words.

NurED article: *kaṭṭigaraga (revision 1786)

Middle Indo-Aryan Source

*kaṭṭigaraga n. m. 'wizard, sorcerer'

Etymology of Source

  • Old Indo-Aryan *kārtikara- 'belonging/relating to a sorcerer/magician' + -ka-, cf.:
    • kŕ̥ti- n. 'action, work; magic'
    • kr̥ti-kara- adj. 'practising magic or enchantment'

Nuristani

  • Katë w, ne kṭírë, se kaṭrë́ n. m. 'wizard, sorcerer'
    • ne kṭíri n. f. 'witch'
    • ne kṭír-vor, se kaṭrë́-vor n. m. 'magic, sorcery'
      [S-kt, SA22 ('جادوگر', 'کوډګر'), S-km]
  • Ashkun s kaṭyerë́ n. m. 'wizard, sorcerer'
    • s kaṭyera-wā́r n. m. 'magic, sorcery'
      [B-w (⟨kaṭirə ~ kaṭerə́⟩, ⟨kaṭerawā́r⟩), Klimburg (1999: 167, 417) (⟨katiˈera⟩, ⟨katiˈerawar⟩)]
  • Prasun p/z k(š)čir(ë) n. 'magic' [⇐ Kt.]
    • + li- 'to do'
    • z/d kščire li- n. 'to practice magic'
      [BD]

Commentary

The reconstruction *kaṭṭi-° presupposed by the attested forms is not directly derivable from OIA kr̥ti-°, from which we would expect something like **kiḍi-°. Instead they more likely reflect a vr̥ddhi form *kārtikara- 'belonging/relating to a sorcerer/magician' derived from kr̥ti-kara-. This adjectival form then seems to have been re-nominalized in the meaning 'sorcerer/magician'. The long vowel of the root syllable is shortened in accordance with the MIA rule of two moras.

The semantic association of the root kar- 'to do' with magic strongly indicates that the word is borrowed from Indo-Aryan, where this association is well attested.

NurED article: *kaṁḍhaga (revision 3399)

Middle Indo-Aryan Source

*kaṁḍhaga n. 'voice, call, invitation; boundary, edge'

Etymology of Source

  • Old Indo-Aryan kaṇṭhá- n. m. 'throat, voice, sound' + -ka-

New Indo-Aryan Cognates

  • Saraiki kā̃ḍhā n. m. 'invitation to a wedding or other feast', kā̃ḍhaṇ v. 'to invite to a wedding, feast etc.'
    [DJWP]
  • Pashai l kāṇḍā n. 'voice, word'
    [IIFL III.3]

For cognates meaning 'boundary, edge' etc., cf. CDIAL (T. 2680)

Nuristani

  • Katë w këṇë́, se kaṇë́ n. 'feast'
    [S-kt; S-km]
    • + amú 'house' (?): ne këṇému n. 'feast'
      [SA22 ('خیرات')]
    • + kṣō- 'to pull, to draw': ne këṇë́ kṣō-, se kaṇë́ kṣō- n. 'to stay' < *'to draw out the feast/invitation' ?
      [SA22 ('to live'); S-km ('stay for a while')]
  • Ashkun s këṇë́ n. 'feast (of merit)'
    [B-w ("Verdienstfest (xeirāt), sowohl in kafirischer, als auch in islamischer Zeit"); S-s]
  • Prasun p/i këṇḍ(ë́) n. 'feast of merit, funeral feast' [⇐ Kt.]
    [BD ("Verdienstfest, Totenfeier (xeirāt)")]
    • + li- 'to do': p/i këṇḍe li- n. 'to hold a feast of merit'
      [BD]
  • Nur. Kalasha ẓ kaṇë́ n. 'boundary, edge, horizon'
    [T]
    • z kaṇë-kaṇë-e n. 'at the edges, at the horizon'
      [T]

Commentary

These words are evidently borrowed from an IA variety with post-nasal voicing, which is known to be present in (parts of) the region since MIA times (cf. Salomon 1999: 129–130; Schoubben 2024: 395–398). This excludes predecessors of the modern-day Gawar-Bati group, but could point to a predecessor of Pashai, though the meaning 'invitation' is not documented there. A cognate without post-nasal voicing (*kaṁṭha) has also been borrowed into Nuristani, possibly from a Gawar-Bati group variety. Notably, the Nuristani forms do not show the NIA lengthening before nasal clusters observable in the Srk. and Pash. forms.

Semantically, a development 'voice' > 'call' > 'invitation (to a feast)' > 'feast' appears to be unproblematic (cf., e.g., Kt. c̣ō ku- 'to call, to invite'). The derivation of the second meaning 'boundary, edge' is more uncertain, but according to Turner (CDIAL: T. 2680) it may be explained as a development from 'throat, neck' via the intermediate meaning 'immediate proximity' attested in the Pañcatantra. Within MIA, Pkt. kaṁṭha- 'border, edge' (cited in CDIAL: T. 2680) attests this meaning.

NurED article: *kaṁṭha (revision 3262)

Middle Indo-Aryan Source

*kaṁṭha n. 'throat, voice, sound'

Etymology of Source

  • Old Indo-Aryan kaṇṭhá- n. m. 'throat, voice, sound'

New Indo-Aryan Cognates

  • Gawar-Bati khaṇṭ n. 'voice, sound'
    [FLI-GB]

Nuristani

  • Katë w/ne/se kuṭ n. m. 'voice, sound; numeral classifier for words'
    [G I-6; S-kt; SA22; Ġ-Q (s.v. غږ); S-km]
  • Ashkun s/t koṭ n. m. 'voice, sound'
    [B-w; M-A2[1]]
  • Prasun p kuṭ n. 'voice' [⇐ Kt.]
    [BD (⟨kọ̄ṭ⟩, ⟨kuṭ⟩)]
    • + Pr. -ug: p kuṭúg n. 'numeral classifier for words; full stop (in writing); word substituted for taboo words'
      [BD]

Commentary

An Indo-Aryan word with no etymology beyond OIA (cf. EWA I: 292). The unconditioned retroflexes make it unlikely that this is an inherited Nuristani word. Borrowed from a source without post-nasal voicing, unlike related *kaṁḍhaga 'voice, call, invitation; boundary, edge'. The sense 'invitation' may have previously also existed for this form, if the element kuṭ in Kt. se kúṭ-miẓō̃ 'feast given when effigy was erected [pre-Islamic]' can be interpreted in this way (miẓō̃́ = 'food eaten with bread').

Turner (CDIAL: T. 2680) also reports a Kt. word "kaṭī́" 'sound' from Morgenstierne's field notes, but this is not known from other sources.

Footnotes

  1. ↑ Buddruss (B-w) clarifies that koṭ in the sentence koṭ ċodei, translated by Morgenstierne (1934: 86) as "the cloud(?) thunders, awāz kēgī", does not mean 'cloud', but 'sound' (= awāz of the Pashto translation).

This group of words originates in a MIA form with early "nasal condensation" (cf. Halfmann 2023b: 330), which has resulted in the preservation of the intervocalic -g-. There are no necessary phonological reasons that would identify these words as borrowed, but the cognates of OIA nāgá- outside of IA mean 'naked' and not 'snake' and other words for snake are more common in the earliest OIA texts, so that the existence of a Nuristani cognate in the meaning 'snake' is not very likely. Additionally, the Nuristani terms appear only in the specialized mythological sense and not as ordinary words for 'snake', which makes it even more likely that they are loanwords.

It is not surprising that the IA word was borrowed only in religious and mythological senses, since in Hinduism "the word for the divine snake is nāga and "worship of the nāga deities associated with water" is one of the well-established forms of Hindu snake worship (Jacobsen 2009: 711). As Jacobsen (2009: 712) explains, "nāgas are connected to water [...] They inhabit lakes and rivers" and "are associated with weather phenomena such as rainstorms and lightening [sic]". These are the same spheres occupied by the etymologically corresponding mythological beings of Nuristani pre-Islamic religion.

The Pr. deity Züzúm, who is identified with Kt. Noŋ, derives his name from an inherited word for *'large reptile', but this may originally have been a calque on the IA word, especially since he is also a god of tempests fitting into the mythological sphere of the nāgas of Hinduism.

The appearance of nāgas in Nuristani pre-Islamic mythology is compatible with the thesis of Halfmann (2023b) that this mythology is largely derived from post-Vedic Hindu models, since nāgá- as the word for 'snake' appears only from the Brāhmaṇas onwards, whereas the earlier Vedic words for snake are áhi- and sarpá- (Jacobsen 2009: 711).

Following Morgenstierne (1949: 279), these Nuristani forms have generally been held to be cognates of OIA vrīhi- 'rice', deriving from a presumable PIIr. form **u̯rīj́hi-. However, it fails both formally, as PIIr. *u̯r- produces Kt. br̆- (cf. br̆e 'flour' < *wre[w]i[ta]-, br̆iċë́- ~ br̆ëċé- 'to spin' < *wriċ-),[1] and semantically, as rice and barley have little in common either in terms of physical attributes or of cultivation techniques. Speakers of ancestral Nuristani varieties are also unlikely to have had knowledge of rice agriculture and its terminology, which was probably borrowed into already diversified Indo-Iranian languages after its arrival in South Asia.

On the other hand, the Khotanese, Tumshuqese and Khwarezmian terms mentioned above produce a plausible formal and semantic match. Kümmel (2017: 281; against Bailey 1979: 367, NEVP: 10) is probably justified in separating these Middle Iranian words from various New Iranian terms that seem to derive from something like *arpućya- or *arpaćya- (e.g. Psht. orbə́ša (f.), Sangl. vərvə́s 'barley', Mnj. āršíya 'type of barley (from central Nuristan)' [NEVP: 10, G-Mnj]).

Some difficulties remain with regard to the vowel development. The i Kt. could derive from an earlier *i, but it may also show the same kind of umlaut before a palatal consonant as in Kt. ◊ piš 'flower' < MIA puśśa. This umlaut would then have to have happened early enough to prevent the outcome ẓ < *r- |_*u. The Pr. form shows additional suffixing and syncope followed by cluster reduction (*rċ/rz > z) and vowel prothesis. Since the prothetic vowel is not a central vowel and has a different quality than the second syllable, it is likely that it reflects the quality of the original root vowel, which would indicate an original *u as the more likely reconstruction.

This matches the Khot. form and also provides a plausible ultimate etymology from the Indo-Iranian root *rau̯ć- ~ *ruć- 'to shine' (OIA rúś-ant- 'shining, bright', Khot. rrus- 'to shine', harśśäñi 'bright' < *fra-ruć-ya-).[2] However, the formation in Nuristani must be different from Khot. – while Khot. s is incompatible with an original cluster *ći̯, the Nuristani forms are best explained from a derivate *rući̯a-, which would account for the umlaut and masculine gender in Kt. and the i in Pr.. The Khwar. and Tumsh. vocalism is then more difficult to reconcile. The form ⟨rsy⟩ (pl.) originally compared to the Khot. form by Henning (1956: 435), was corrected to ⟨rysy⟩ in Henning (1958: 114, fn. 9 - "rysy wahrscheinlich statt rsy 'Gerste' zu lesen"). While a spelling with no written vowel would have been compatible with the assumption of a root vowel u, the spelling with ⟨y⟩, which also appears in the singular, would rather point to ī or e. Umlaut of *ū̆ > ī̆ seems, however, to be otherwise unattested in Khwar.. The vocalism of the Tumsh. form is already unexpected when compared to closely related Khot.. This issue is also discussed by Ogihara & Ching (2024) and Halfmann (2026: 298).

Since Morgenstierne (1929: 284), these Nuristani forms have been connected with PIE *u̯erh1- 'to say' (Gr. εἴρω). Based on this, Turner (CDIAL: T. 11327) reconstructed a Pseudo-OIA form *vari- 'speech', but this could not account for the -r-, which, in an inherited word, should be dropped in intervocalic position. His proposal of connections with OIA varṇa- 'sound, syllable' and vā́ṇī- 'voice, sound' is doubtful, as the former is more likely a specialized use of varṇa- 'type, color' and the latter already appears as vāṇī- in the R̥gveda, which makes it rather implausible to assume a reduction from *varṇī vel sim., as would be required for a connection with the other words (cf. KEWA III: 154, 184). It is also difficult to reconcile with the laryngeal which is nowadays reconstructed in PIE *u̯erh1-.

On the other hand, a connection with the Indo-European word for 'word', which likely contains the same PIE root, could account for the -r- as a reflex of *-rr- < *-rd-. The only issue with this explanation is that this etymon does not otherwise appear in Indo-Iranian. Though the Kt. forms could equally well descend from a form with PIIr. *ar or *r̥ in the first syllable, in A. the development to *-rr- would not be expected if the root had *r̥ (cf. A. židí < PIIr. *j́hr̥dai̯a-). A reconstruction with *ar is therefore more likely. The final vowel may reflect a suffix *-iya- or *-ika-.

This suffix is attested since the Middle Iranian period (e.g. MP šāh-wār 'like a king') (see Durkin-Meisterernst 2014: 182) and has been adopted for language names in various cases, e.g. in dialectal Tajik vanǰi-vorí 'in Vanji' = "like the Vanjis" (Steblin-Kamenskij 1999: 391) and (as a loanword) in Domari ḍōm-wāri 'the Domari language', tat-wāri 'the Arabic language' (Matras 2012: 4). Horn (1893: 240) separates it etymologically from homonymous -wār 'bearing' < *-bāra- (as, e.g., in NP umēd-wār 'hopeful'), but Durkin-Meisterernst (2014: 182) makes no such distinction. The Nuristani forms, by contrast, are not suffixes, but frequently appear in independent use. They also cannot derive from a form with long *ā in the first syllable.
